questions.question: Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoans of which genus?
questions.explanation: Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Leishmania, which are obligate intracellular parasites of macrophages.

questions.question: Which family do Leishmania parasites belong to?
questions.explanation: Leishmania belongs to the family Trypanosomidae, alongside the trypanosomes — both are flagellated protozoa transmitted by insect vectors.

questions.question: What are the only known vectors of leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Phlebotomine sandflies are the only known vectors of leishmaniasis. Only the female sandfly transmits the parasite when taking a blood meal.

questions.question: How many main clinical syndromes does leishmaniasis consist of?
questions.explanation: Leishmaniasis presents as four main clinical syndromes: visceral, cutaneous, muco-cutaneous, and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis.

questions.question: Which is not a main clinical syndrome of leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary is not a recognised main clinical syndrome of leishmaniasis. The four recognised syndromes are visceral, cutaneous, muco-cutaneous, and PKDL.

questions.question: Muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis is also known as what?
questions.explanation: Muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis is also known as espundia — it involves destruction of the mucous membranes of the nose, mouth, and throat.

questions.question: Visceral leishmaniasis is also known as what?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis is also known as kala-azar, meaning "black sickness" — a reference to the darkening of the skin seen in some patients.

questions.question: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis is characterized by what type of rash?
questions.explanation: PKDL is characterised by a macular, maculo-papular, or nodular rash — typically appearing on the face and trunk months to years after treated kala-azar.

questions.question: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis is a complication of which condition?
questions.explanation: PKDL is a complication of visceral leishmaniasis, appearing after apparent cure of the visceral disease. It serves as a reservoir of infection for sandflies.

questions.question: Which species is responsible for most cases of muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Leishmania braziliensis is the main cause of muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis, primarily found in South and Central America.

questions.question: Kala-azar is caused by which Leishmania species?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is caused by L. donovani or L. infantum. L. donovani is anthroponotic; L. infantum is zoonotic with dogs as the main reservoir.

questions.question: Which is a synonym for visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Dumdum fever is a synonym for visceral leishmaniasis, named after Dum Dum, a town near Kolkata, India, where the disease was first described.

questions.question: Visceral leishmaniasis is characterized by irregular fever, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, emaciation, anaemia, and what?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis is characterised by irregular fever, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, emaciation, anaemia, and leucopaenia — the parasite suppresses bone marrow function.

questions.question: Indian kala-azar is endemic in which region?
questions.explanation: Indian kala-azar is endemic in Eastern India, particularly in Bihar, West Bengal, and neighbouring states along the Ganges plain.

questions.question: Mediterranean kala-azar is often referred to as what?
questions.explanation: Mediterranean kala-azar is also called infantile kala-azar because it predominantly affects young children, caused by L. infantum.

questions.question: Over 90% of visceral leishmaniasis cases occur in how many countries?
questions.explanation: Over 90% of global visceral leishmaniasis cases occur in six countries: Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Sudan, Ethiopia, and Brazil.

questions.question: Which is not one of the six countries with majority of VL cases?
questions.explanation: Nigeria is not among the six countries with the highest visceral leishmaniasis burden. The six are Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Sudan, Ethiopia, and Brazil.

questions.question: L. donovani infects which age groups?
questions.explanation: L. donovani infects all age groups. Unlike L. infantum, which predominantly affects children, L. donovani causes disease across the age spectrum.

questions.question: L. infantum infects mostly which group?
questions.explanation: L. infantum mostly infects children and immunosuppressed individuals — its synonym "infantile kala-azar" reflects the age pattern in Mediterranean regions.

questions.question: Which factor drives increased incidence of visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: HIV co-infection drives increased incidence of visceral leishmaniasis. HIV and Leishmania each worsen the other, and co-infected patients are highly infectious to sandflies.

questions.question: What are the three essential factors for transmission of kala-azar?
questions.explanation: Transmission of kala-azar requires three essential factors: a reservoir (human or animal), the vector (phlebotomine sandfly), and a susceptible population.

questions.question: What is the main reservoir of L. infantum in zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Dogs are the main reservoir of L. infantum in zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis. Infected dogs provide the source from which sandflies acquire the parasite.

questions.question: In India, what is the only reservoir of kala-azar?
questions.explanation: In India, the only reservoir of kala-azar is man — the disease is anthroponotic. No animal reservoir has been identified in the Indian subcontinent.

questions.question: Which sandfly is the main vector of kala-azar in India?
questions.explanation: Phlebotomus argentipes is the main vector of kala-azar in India. It is zoophilic and feeds readily on humans in endemic areas.

questions.question: Which form of L. donovani is found in the gut of the arthropod vector?
questions.explanation: The promastigote form (with a free flagellum) is found in the gut of the sandfly vector. It is the infective form injected into the mammalian host.

questions.question: Which form of L. donovani develops intracellularly in the mammalian host?
questions.explanation: The amastigote form (without a free flagellum) develops intracellularly inside macrophages in the mammalian host. It multiplies by binary fission.

questions.question: Only which sex of phlebotomine sandflies transmit leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Only female sandflies transmit leishmaniasis — they require a blood meal for egg development, and it is during this feeding that they inject promastigotes.

questions.question: Visceral leishmaniasis is essentially a disease of which system?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis is essentially a disease of the reticuloendothelial system — the parasite multiplies in macrophages of the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

questions.question: The incubation period of visceral leishmaniasis generally lasts how long?
questions.explanation: The incubation period of visceral leishmaniasis generally lasts 2 to 6 months, though it can range from 10 days to several years.

questions.question: Enlarged lymph nodes are rarely found in which kala-azar patients?
questions.explanation: Enlarged lymph nodes are rarely found in Indian kala-azar patients. Lymphadenopathy is more common in Sudanese and other African forms.

questions.question: Hyper-pigmentation has only been described in patients from which country?
questions.explanation: Hyper-pigmentation — the darkening of skin that gave kala-azar its name "black sickness" — has only been described in patients from India.

questions.question: The aldehyde test detects what in visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: The aldehyde test detects polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, which causes serum proteins to gel when formalin is added. It is a nonspecific but useful screening test.

questions.question: Which test is the classical confirmatory test for visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Microscopic examination of aspirates — from spleen, bone marrow, or lymph node — is the classical confirmatory test for visceral leishmaniasis, showing amastigotes within macrophages.

questions.question: Sensitivity of microscopy is highest for which aspirate?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity of microscopy is highest for spleen aspirate (about 93–99%), followed by bone marrow (53–86%) and lymph node (53–65%).

questions.question: Which drug was the first effective oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Miltefosine was the first effective oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis, originally developed as an anticancer agent and later found to be active against Leishmania.

questions.question: Which drug replaced antimonials as first-line treatment in some areas of India?
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B replaced antimonials as first-line treatment in some areas of India after widespread antimony resistance emerged in Bihar.

questions.question: Which is a pentavalent antimonial used for visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Sodium stibogluconate is a pentavalent antimonial — the traditional first-line drug for visceral leishmaniasis, though resistance has developed in some regions.

questions.question: What is the suggested way forward for treatment of visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Combination therapy is the suggested way forward — pairing drugs with different mechanisms prevents resistance and shortens treatment duration.

questions.question: Which control strategy is used for visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Reservoir and vector control is the main strategy — targeting infected dogs (in zoonotic areas) and the sandfly vector through indoor residual spraying.

questions.question: Deltamethrine-treated collars are used to reduce infection in what?
questions.explanation: Deltamethrin-treated collars reduce infection in dogs — the main reservoir for L. infantum in zoonotic visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.question: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is also known as what?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is also known as oriental sore — a self-healing skin lesion caused by various Leishmania species.

questions.question: The aetiologic agent of cutaneous leishmaniasis is which species?
questions.explanation: Leishmania tropica is the main aetiologic agent of Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis, along with L. major and L. aethiopica.

questions.question: L. tropica major causes which type of leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: L. tropica major causes moist (rural) cutaneous leishmaniasis — the lesions are wet, ulcerate early, and heal relatively quickly.

questions.question: L. tropica minor causes which type of leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: L. tropica minor causes dry (urban) cutaneous leishmaniasis — lesions are dry, ulcerate late, and heal slowly.

questions.question: Which vector transmits L. tropica major from rodents to man?
questions.explanation: Phlebotomus papatasi transmits L. tropica major from rodents to man. It is the main vector of rural cutaneous leishmaniasis in the Middle East.

questions.question: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis in Ethiopia and Kenya is caused by which species?
questions.explanation: Leishmania aethiopica causes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis in Ethiopia and Kenya, characterised by non-ulcerating nodules all over the body.

questions.question: In cutaneous leishmaniasis, the incubation period in the moist form is how long?
options: Many months to over a year
questions.explanation: In the moist (rural) form of cutaneous leishmaniasis, the incubation period is short — a few weeks to a few months.

questions.question: In the dry form of cutaneous leishmaniasis, lesions last for how long?
questions.explanation: In the dry (urban) form, lesions last for many months — up to a year or more — before healing, leaving depressed scars.

questions.question: Uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis ulcers heal within how long?
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis ulcers heal within two months to a year, leaving a permanent scar. They are often self-limiting.

questions.question: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by which species?
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is caused by L. braziliensis, which produces destructive lesions of the mucous membranes of the nose, mouth, and pharynx.
